description.narrative: Dreketi Primary School was one of the most severely affected schools by the category 5 Tropical Cyclone Yasa in December 2020, which damaged all but one classroom. For three years (2021- 2023), students utilised tents as their classrooms, which was a challenging learning environment for the students given the heat, humidity and rainy weather. For the 200 students at the school, the six new classrooms and ablution block built by the Cyclone Recovery Program, and completed in time for the 2024 school year, provides a conducive and climate resilient learning environment. The new buildings are certified to withstand category 5 tropical cyclone, built from locally sourced materials, equipped with rainwater harvesting and solar power, have accessibility ramps and washrooms, and can be reconfigured to serve as community evacuation centres.

In 2024, Cyclone Yasa Recovery Program (CRP) rehabilitated infrastructure in nine priority schools in Vanua Levu as well as undertook the detailed design for the upgrades of Taveuni and Kadavu hospitals.. The program integrates elements of the six G20 Principles for Quality Infrastructure Investment into all infrastructure. ‍ To ensure positive spillover effects from the program, CRP restricted tenders for design and construction to locally registered firms and required contractors to employ workers from local communities, so that the benefits were retained in the local economy. Environmental, climate and disaster resilience considerations included cyclone resilient standards and certifications, mandatory environmental assessments, and disaster resilience trainings. The inclusion of disability audits and accessibility ramps were mandatory for all school works undertaken by the program. Social procurement was included to maximise the benefits for the local community members. Finally, CRP was designed to ensure strengthened and inclusive governance. This included having a quality assurance supervisor to ensure that the works were done in a timely manner and included all relevant stakeholders in decision-making processes. Moreover, the program had appropriate safeguards mechanisms in place to ensure contractors were fully informed of their responsibilities and adhered to DFAT’s Environmental and Social Safeguard Policy.

description.narrative: In 2024, the Tropical Cyclone Yasa Recovery Program (CRP) is rehabilitating infrastructure in nine schools in Vanua Levu and the Taveuni and Kadavu hospitals, which were damaged by Tropical Cyclone Yasa in December 2020 and Tropical Cyclone Ana in January 2021. The new school buildings were designed to withstand category five tropical cyclones, and the refurbished buildings to withstand category three tropical cyclones. School upgrades also included rainwater harvesting tanks, solar power, accessibility ramps and washrooms. Further, the classrooms have been designed to be reconfigured as community evacuation centres. Seven schools were completed during the reporting period. ‍ CRP collaborated with Australia's Disaster Resilience Program (DRP) to build Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) capacity at four CRP schools. CRP implemented training on disaster preparations related to putting up and taking down cyclone shutters and safely removing solar panels during cyclones. For the two hospitals a climate resilient infrastructure masterplan was delivered. During the reporting period, further detailed designs and scope of works were confirmed.

Supporting locally led development was a core component of the program, with careful considerations made to enhance localisation. The program only utilised Fiji-registered contractors and suppliers for the school and hospital infrastructure, as well as the furnishings, to maximise benefits of the program to the local community. This included design, construction and supervision contractors. ‍ CRP also mandated construction contractors to employ all unskilled labour from the school communities. Through CRP’s social procurement policy, men and women from the school communities generated income through the sale of fresh produce and fish.The program also procured traditionally woven mats from women’s groups from local communities as a targeted opportunity for women. The social procurement initiatives provided additional income generation opportunities for community members. ‍ For example, Peni Vuniwai*, a carpenter from a local village, joined Capital Construction's team at Ratu Luke Memorial School. The job helped him to improve his family's financial situation. Peni’s long-term goal is to use his earnings from this job to extend and paint his house. ‍ *name has been changed to protect identity

The Cyclone Recovery Program (CRP) developed masterplans for Kadavu and Taveuni Hospitals through consultations with hospital management and the Ministry of Health and Medical Services (MHMS) to identify priority works. ‍ The two master plans enabled DFAT and the Ministry of Health and Medical Services to select and fund infrastructure works at the hospitals. Subsequently, detailed designs were developed for the hospitals works. These detailed designs identified infrastructure works and provided cost estimates that can be implemented throughout the program. These included roof maintenance, general electrical and hydraulics upgrades, and building accessibility ramps. ‍ These repair works will contribute towards the safe and continuous function of hospital services to meet local demand. Once completed, these hospitals will serve the entire populations living on Kadavu and Taveuni and serve as the primary healthcare facilities for the islands.

The Cyclone Recovery Program (CRP) is rehabilitating infrastructure in nine priority schools in Vanua Levu and the Taveuni and Kadavu hospitals. The program integrates elements of the six G20 Principles for Quality Infrastructure Investment. To stimulate the local economy, CRP restricted tenders for design and construction to locally registered firms and required the contractors to employ workers from the local communities. Environmental, climate and disaster resilience considerations included cyclone resilient standards and certifications, mandatory environmental assessments, and disaster resilience trainings and discussions. To integrate social considerations, inclusion of disability audits and accessibility ramps are mandatory for all schools and hospitals work undertaken by the program and social procurement was included to maximise the benefits for the local community members. Finally, CRP included mechanisms to ensure strengthened and inclusive governance by including all relevant stakeholders in decision-making processes.

The Cyclone Recovery Program (CRP) is undertaking infrastructure rehabilitation of the Taveuni and Kadavu hospitals, both of which sustained damage from Tropical Cyclone Yasa. During the reporting period, a high quality, phased and costed, infrastructure master plan was delivered for each hospital. The two master plans will allow DFAT, the Ministry of Health and Medical Services, and other donors to select and fund infrastructure works at the hospitals. For CRP, the masterplan has identified infrastructure works and provided cost estimates that can be implemented through the program. These include roof maintenance, general electrical and hydraulics upgrades and building accessibility ramps.

description.narrative: The Tropical Cyclone Yasa Recovery Program's (CRP) school project is supporting 1,547 students and 78 staff from nine schools by building climate resilient school facilities. CRP’s contractors built or refurbished classroom buildings, accessible toilet blocks, administration buildings with sickbays, canteens, dormitories, dining halls with kitchens and staff quarters across nine schools in Vanua Levu. The works also included the construction of covered walkways and footpaths connecting all the buildings. ‍ All school buildings were designed to be resilient and withstand tropical cyclones. New buildings were built to withstand category 5 cyclones through the use of robust concrete footings, extensive strapping connecting roof trusses to walls and heavy-duty window protectors. Existing buildings were refurbished to withstand category 3 cyclones. These buildings also feature resource management systems, including solar panels and rainwater tanks with harvesting systems. The new buildings could also be used as evacuation centres during disasters. ‍ Passive energy features, such as insulation, natural lighting, cross ventilation and strategic orientation, were incorporated to reduce energy use and keep classrooms cooler. In May 2024, CRP monitored temperature differences between the internal and external environments across five schools. The study found that internal environments were, on average, two degrees cooler than the outside.
